title: The Hangul museum is closed — the shows moved
subtitle: hangul year · shut until 2028
why_trust: A fire during rooftop construction in February 2025 closed the National Hangul Museum, and the reopening target is October 2028. Every guidebook and blog still sends you to Yongsan, where you now find a construction hoarding beside the National Museum of Korea. Meanwhile the museum has designated 2026 its 'Year of Hangul' — 100 years since Hangul Day was first declared, 580 since Hunminjeongeum was published — and is running its anniversary exhibitions inside other institutions, including the National Folk Museum by Gyeongbokgung. The programming is real. The address isn't.
order_tip: Check hangeul.go.kr for the current host venue before you build a day around it. If you just want the script material, the National Museum of Korea next door has it permanently, free, with English labels.
avoid_if: Skip the Yongsan trip entirely if the museum was your only reason — there is nothing to see behind the fence.

title: October gives Seoul two long weekends
subtitle: seasonal moment · public holidays
why_trust: Gaecheonjeol falls on Saturday 3 October, which pushes a substitute holiday onto Monday the 5th; Hangul Day is Friday 9 October. That is two consecutive three-day weekends inside one month, and Koreans travel on both of them. Domestic flights, hanok stays and any restaurant that takes bookings go first; palaces, Seongsu and Bukchon carry local crowds on top of the tourist ones. The trade is real, though — department stores and cafés run their best seasonal menus and events precisely on those dates.
order_tip: Book stays and any table you actually care about three weeks out, and keep the 6th to 8th for whatever you want quiet.
avoid_if: If crowds ruin a trip for you and your dates are flexible, come the week of 12 October instead — same autumn weather, half the queue.

title: Hangul is the souvenir, not the T-shirt
subtitle: city collab · October drops
why_trust: Every autumn Korean jewellery houses release Hangul pieces for the holiday. J.ESTINA's line uses the official Seoul city typeface — ㅎㄱ for hangul, ㅅㅇ for Seoul — engraved on 925 silver bracelets, ear cuffs and earrings. Golden Dew has worked with Ahn Sang-soo, the most consequential typographer in the country, on a heritage collection built from the letter ㅎ. These are designed for the domestic market and only secondarily for visitors, which is precisely why they read as jewellery instead of merchandise.
order_tip: Department store jewellery floors from late September. Limited editions are usually gone by mid-October, and the ear cuffs go before the bracelets.
avoid_if: Skip it under about ₩100,000 — below that the Hangul souvenir is printed keyrings, and it looks like it.
